etymologies.etymologyHTML: Derived from Old French divorce, from Latin dīvortium, from dīvertere (“to turn aside”), from dī- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

definitions.definition: The legal dissolution of a marriage.

quote.citation: 2019 November 21, Samanth Subramanian, “How our home delivery habit reshaped the world”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: The great trick of online retail has been to get us to do more shopping while thinking less about it – thinking less, in particular, about how our purchases reach our homes. This divorce of a product from its voyage to us is perhaps the thing that Amazon has sold us most successfully

quote.citation: c. 1599, William Shakespeare, Henry V, act 5, scene 2:
quote.text: To make divorce of their incorporate league

definitions.definition: (zoology) The separation of a bonded pair of animals.

quote.citation: c. 1613, William Shakespeare, John Fletcher, Henry VIII, act 2, scene 1:
quote.text: Go with me like good angels to my end; / And as the long divorce of steel falls on me, / Make of your prayers one sweet sacrifice, / And lift my soul to heaven. Lead on, o' God's name.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To legally dissolve a marriage between two people.
(transitive) To end one's own marriage to (a person) in this way.
(transitive) To separate something that was connected.

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Twelfe Night, or What You Will”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv], page 269:
quote.text: He is knight dubb'd with vnhatche'd Rapier, and on carpet conſideration, but he is a diuell in priuate brall, soules and bodies hath he diuorc'd three, and his incenſement at this moment is ſo implacable, that ſatisfaction can be none, but by pangs of death and ſepulcher: Hob, nob, is his word: giu't or take't.
